{{Short description|Mathematical concept in homotopy theory}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[homotopy theory]], '''Ken Brown's lemma''' gives a sufficient condition for a [[functor]] on a category of [[fibrant object]]s to preserve [[weak equivalence (homotopy theory)|weak equivalence]]s; the sufficient condition is that acyclic fibrations go to weak equivalences.<ref>{{harv|Cisinski|2019|loc=Proposition 7.4.13}}</ref><ref>{{harv|factorization lemma in nLab|loc=Proposition 3.1.}}</ref> The dual of the statement also holds. The lemma or, more precisely, a result of which the lemma is a corollary, was introduced by [[Kenneth Brown (mathematician)|Kenneth Brown]].<ref>Kenneth Brown, p. 421 (4 of 41) in: Abstract Homotopy Theory and Generalized Sheaf Cohomology, 1973, p. 4</ref>

== Proof ==
The lemma follows from the following:

{{math_theorem|name=Factorization lemma|math_statement=Let <math>f</math> be a morphism in a given category of fibrant objects. Then <math>f</math> factorizes as <math>f = g \circ j</math> where
*<math>g</math> is a fibration,
*<math>j</math> admits a retract that is an acyclic fibration.}}

To see the lemma follows from the above, let <math>w</math> be a weak equivalence and <math>F</math> the given functor. By the factorization lemma, we can write
:<math>w = g \circ j</math>
with an acyclic fibration <math>r</math> such that <math>r \circ j = \operatorname{id}</math>. Note <math>j</math> is a weak equivalence since <math>r</math> is. Thus, <math>g</math> is a weak equivalence (thus acyclic fibration) since <math>w</math> is. So, <math>F(g)</math> is a weak equivalence by assumption. Similarly, <math>F(j)</math> is a weak equivalence. Hence, <math>F(w) = F(g) \circ F(j)</math> is a weak equivalence. <math>\square</math>

''Proof of factorization lemma'': Let <math>f : X \to Y</math> be the given morphism. Let
:<math>e : Y^I \to Y \times Y</math>
be the [[path object fibration]]; namely, it is obtained by factorizing the diagonal map <math>\Delta</math> as <math>\Delta = e \circ c</math> where <math>c</math> is a weak equivalence.

Then let <math>\pi : Z \to X \times Y</math> be the pull-back of <math>e</math> along <math>f \times \operatorname{id}</math>, which is again a fibration. Then by the [[universal property]] of the pull-back, we get a map <math>j : X \to Z</math> so that the resulting diagram with <math>X \overset{f}\to Y \overset{c}\to Y^I</math> and <math>(\operatorname{id}_X, f)</math> commutes. Take <math>g</math> to be <math>Z \overset{\pi}\to X \times Y \overset{p_2}\to Y</math>, which is a fibration since the projection <math>p_2</math> is the pull-back of the fibration <math>Y \to </math> final object.

As for <math>j</math>, let <math>r</math> be <math>Z \overset{\pi}\to X \times Y \overset{p_1}\to X</math>, which is again a fibration. Note that <math>r</math> is the pull-back of <math>q \circ e : Y^I \to Y</math>, <math>q</math> a projection. Since <math>e \circ c = \Delta</math>, we have <math>q \circ e \circ c = \operatorname{id}</math>. It follows <math>q \circ e</math> is a weak equivalence (since <math>c</math> is) and thus <math>r</math> is a weak equivalence. <math>\square</math>
